name: String.split()
desc: Splits a string on a regular expression and returns the fields as an array. The limit argument decides what happens to empty trailing fields.
body:
The argument is a regex, not a plain separator. Characters with a meaning in a pattern have to be escaped, and `Pattern.quote(separator)` does that for an arbitrary string.

The limit argument has three useful values. Zero or omitted drops empty trailing fields, which hides a missing column. A negative number keeps every field, so the array length always matches the column count. A positive number splits at most that many times, which is how a field that itself contains the separator survives.

Read the fields with the index you expect only after you check the length. A short row is the normal way a CSV parser throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` in an exam.

name: String.join() and formatted()
desc: Joins fields with a separator and formats a template with positional arguments. Both replace a hand written StringBuilder for short text.

name: StringBuilder in a loop
desc: Appends into one growable buffer instead of copying the string on every pass. Required when a loop builds a report line by line.
body:
`append` returns the same builder, so the calls chain. `toString` copies the buffer at that moment: a later append cannot change the string you already took, which is why printing a snapshot and printing the builder differ.

A builder is not thread safe. If two threads append, wrap the writes in a `synchronized` block or use `StringBuffer`, which is the synchronized version of the same class.

name: Arrays.sort() and binarySearch()
desc: Sorts an array in place and searches a sorted array. The search only works after the sort, and a miss returns a negative insertion point.
body:
Primitive arrays take no comparator. For a descending `int[]` there are two normal choices: sort ascending and walk it backwards, or box the values into an `Integer[]` and pass `Comparator.reverseOrder()`.

`Arrays.toString` prints one dimension. A nested array needs `Arrays.deepToString`, otherwise you see the reference of each row.

name: LocalDate plusDays() and ChronoUnit
desc: Moves a date by a number of days and counts the days between two dates. LocalDate is immutable, so every change returns a new object.

name: DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern()
desc: Builds a display and parse format from a pattern. The same formatter must be used to read the text back, and a locale fixes month names.
body:
`yyyy` is the calendar year and `YYYY` is the week based year, which can differ around January. `MM` is the month and `mm` is the minute. `dd` is the day of the month and `DD` is the day of the year. Those four swaps produce output that looks right until the date is near a boundary.

Formatting a date and parsing it back with the same formatter is a cheap round trip test. If the parsed value differs, the pattern is missing a field the text carries.

name: record with a compact constructor
desc: Declares an immutable data class and validates the components in a compact constructor. The compiler writes the accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString.
body:
The compact form repeats the component list only in the header. Inside the body you assign to the parameter name, and the compiler writes the field assignment after your code, so a normalised value is what gets stored.

Records cannot extend a class, cannot declare extra instance fields, and are final. They can implement an interface, which is enough for the exam tasks that ask for a sortable or printable row.

name: Scanner nextInt() and nextLine()
desc: Reads whitespace separated tokens or a whole line. The hasNext method guards the read, and nextLine after nextInt needs one extra call.
body:
`Scanner` reads tokens, not records. A file with one field per line therefore needs `nextLine` plus a `split` rather than a chain of `next` calls, unless the order of the fields is fixed and the file has no blank lines.

Close a scanner that wraps a file or a stream. Closing a scanner over `System.in` also closes the shared stream, which matters in a program that reads twice.

name: enum with fields and methods
syntax: enum Type { A(1), B(2); private final int x; }
desc: Gives each constant its own data through a private constructor. The constant list comes first, fields and methods after it.

name: Generic method with a bound
syntax: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items)
desc: Declares a type parameter and limits it to comparable types, so the body may call compareTo and the return type stays concrete.
body:
Without the bound, `compareTo` is not a method of `T` and the body does not compile. With the bound, the compiler knows the argument implements `Comparable` of itself.

Type parameters are erased at run time. That is why `new T[]`, `instanceof T`, and `T.class` fail, and why a generic class cannot have a static field of type `T`.

name: Executors.newFixedThreadPool()
desc: Runs submitted tasks on a fixed number of reused threads. shutdown and awaitTermination end the pool and wait for the running work.

name: HashMap.merge() for counting
desc: Adds a value to a key, creating it when absent. It is the shortest counting idiom and removes the get, null check, put sequence.
body:
The third argument is a `BiFunction` that receives the old value and the new one. `Integer::sum` is the common case. For a map of lists, `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value)` is the matching idiom.

A map has no iteration order. Print a report by sorting the entries into a list, not by trusting `entrySet`.

name: HashSet duplicate check
desc: Stores unique values and reports a duplicate through the boolean result of add. No order is kept and null is allowed once.

name: switch expression
desc: Returns a value from a switch, with no fallthrough. A block case returns with yield, and an enum switch must cover every constant.

name: var for local variables
desc: Infers the type of a local variable from its initialiser. The type is fixed at compile time and the variable stays strongly typed.
body:
`var` is syntax for the compiler, not a type. `var x = 0;` declares an `int` and assigning a string later is the same error as with an explicit type.

Use it when the right side already spells the type, as in `var rows = new ArrayList<Booking>()`. Avoid it when the right side hides the type behind a method call, because the reader then has to open that method.
